newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Oppn sets out stand on native title.
newsitem.headline: Australian Oppn sets out stand on native title.

text.p: Australian Opposition Leader Kim Beazley on Tuesday set out what he called the key elements of his Labor Party's approach to native title, an issue that farmers and miners say is damaging their industries.

"These elements will guide our response to any government decision, although no final position on any government proposals to amend the Native Title Act will be determined until the release of detailed draft legislation," Beazley said in a statement.
The High Court ruled in December that Aborigines had unspecified rights to share land that the government had leased to pastoralists.
Since the Aborigines' rights are uncertain, farmers are demanding the government clarify the situation in legislation, preferably by abolishing native title on the leases.
Many mines also operate on pastoral leases.
Beazley rejected abolition, however, and his stand would make it difficult for the government to get such legislation through the Senate, the upper house of parliament.
The opposition leader listed his "key elements" as:
-- Fair reconciliation of the interests of Aborigines, pastoralists, miners and taxpayers.

-- "Legislative extinguishment of those (native title) rights, as they now co-exist on pastoral leases, whether direct or de facto, would necessarily be discriminatory and unacceptable on moral, legal and financial grounds." (The constitution demands that the government compensate people if it takes their property.)

-- The Native Title Act, which governs such land claims, might have to be amended to clarify things, but it would generally be better for lessees and Aborigines to negotiate the terms of co-existence, rather than have them imposed.
-- The law should prevent unrealistic land claims from being even registered.

-- Any uncertainty over pastoral use of the leases should be removed and other agricultural uses could be permitted as long as native title was not abolished and as long as there was compensation for any rights that were lost.

-- "The mining and petroleum industry should have clear, efficient and timely processes available to them to enable exploration and development to proceed compatibly with native title interests where negotiated agreements cannot be quickly or easily achieved." Different industries would want to gain the necessary rights at different stages of their projects and the legislation would have to provide for that.
-- Legislation should validate land entitlements that had been mistakenly made since 1994 on the assumption that pastoral leases had abolished native title.
The government is trying to produce a policy to clarify and regulate native title on pastoral leases.
Prime Minister John Howard briefed cabinet on the issue on Tuesday but no policy was finalised.
The former Labor government reacted to the original invention of native title in 1992 by the High Court with the Native Title Act.
But the Native Title Act -- the result of acrimonious negotiations with farmers, miners, aborigines and other political parties -- assumed that native title would not exist on pastoral leases.
In the 1996 Wik decision the court ruled that it did.
